en: The Sūtra of One Hundred Parables in Verse on the Conversion of the World by Jayasena,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mingjiao, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject [to the Emperor], at the Mi-lin Monastery in Jālandhara, Central India.
The sages of the past, such as Kāśyapa and others, have left no scriptural verses unspoken;
now I shall recite these gāthās myself to delight the minds of the ignorant, summarizing them as "A Hundred Parables."
Practicing kindness, practicing righteousness, and practicing noble virtue; being without self, without pride, and without cowardice;
possessing true compassion and worthy of being honored as a teacher—one is fit to be a superior person who practices the path of transcendence.
Though poor and lowly, he maintains a firm resolve; even when placed in wealth and honor, he remains gentle and flexible.
When encountering a powerful adversary, he displays courage and strength—this is what is called the mark of a Great Man.
Young men who practice virtue are rare; those who give with joy when asked for something, or who feel shame upon hearing themselves praised—such people are likewise difficult to find.
If you wish to seek a good reputation, first seek the Dharma; when the mind is refined within the Dharma, virtue arises naturally.
Those who strictly and secretly uphold all precepts and practices are exceedingly rare in this world.
One whose natural disposition is virtuous and whose speech is also virtuous—such a person is fully known by both the good and the wicked;
one who conceals the faults of others when they may exist—such a wise person is rare in this world.
The nature of fire is warmth and is inherently hot; the nature of the moon is coolness, and it is likewise so.
The Kṣatriya caste is renowned as superior; how could those of lower castes find this strange?
When one's own kin face peril and require rescue, and when others likewise encounter hardship,
to exert one’s full strength for them with an impartial heart— this is called "right livelihood" within this context.
Generosity, patience, and the power of wisdom, along with mastery over the senses and excellence in speech—these are the true adornments of the noble ones;
the adornment of gold and jewels is like carrying a heavy burden.
There has never been a single thing in the world That is not destroyed and rendered empty by impermanence;
Only the virtue of unconditioned tranquility Remains eternally constant, steadfast through kalpas.
Excellent is your form and body, so upright and handsome; you possess the radiant light of sublime cultivated virtue.
Like the bright moon suspended in the sky, your pure radiance illuminates the pavilions.
The wealthy and noble practice generosity toward all people; with a discerning mind, they accomplish boundless dharmas.
With courageous strength, they rescue and protect the weak and lowly—how excellent is this virtue, truly wholesome!
The virtuous cherish virtue and pity the lack thereof; the foolish disregard virtue and abandon it.
Wisdom is like the crimson sun emitting blazing light, while folly resembles the starlight that obscures its brilliance.
The wise are able to guard themselves against all transgressions; by single-mindedly cultivating and honoring them, their virtuous conduct becomes sublime.
Yet, if they allow their minds even a moment’s indulgence and commit a single fault, the many virtues accumulated through long cultivation will all be lost.
The wicked person distances themselves from the virtue of the precepts and constantly desires to associate with those who are unwholesome;
it is like abandoning a cool pool of merit and entering turbid, impure water.
One applies oil to the body to remove dirt, yet to remove that dirt one must wash away the oil;
just as when performing a task one seeks its successful completion, once the work is finished, one abandons what was done.
The wicked person is ever-wicked, like a black serpent; The wicked person is deluded and dissolute, like a rutting elephant.
The virtuous person feels fear and heartache, While the wicked person, in their perversion, feels joy.
A great fire reaching to the heavens is difficult to extinguish; a deep precipice with no bottom cannot be fathomed.
With discerning wisdom, one should carefully observe perilous and evil matters; practicing deeply and trusting in the good, one remains free from doubt and slander.
Falling from a cliff or entering a fire is a great peril; one might survive and rise again to walk.
But if a person falls into the miserable realms (*apāya*), that deep abyss of the miserable realms cannot be escaped.
It cannot be swept away by great floods or surging waves; it cannot be burned by the fierce flames of a great fire;
it cannot be plundered by a host of violent thieves—this is the supreme wealth of the world.
The base person relies on wealth; the person of middle quality has nothing to rely upon.
The person of middling capacity feels a slight joy at seeing wealth, but the base person regards wealth as the highest thing in the world.

All lineages, physical forms, and virtues; fellow practitioners, kinsmen, and friends—each one does not know from whence they come, yet they strive only for greed, folly, and the pursuit of wealth and profit.
The wealthy speak falsehoods as truth, while the poor speak truth yet are treated as wrongdoers;
they are sycophantic, deceitful, and arrogant, lacking true conduct—when the virtuous and good hear this, they feel shame.
One may possess wealth and noble status yet lack virtue; this is like praising a person who possesses virtue.
One may be poor and lowly yet complete in virtuous conduct; yet the ignorant, lacking wisdom, slander and revile them.
His courageous conduct is as if non-existent; this is the true contemplation of that virtuous person.
Detached from wealth, he dwells peacefully in the path of pure poverty; his kinsmen treat his poverty with disdain, regarding it as a mere delusion.
The butcher praises his wealth and status as true, yet the noble man is deemed base for having no riches;
relatives and friends follow worldly sentiments, honoring the butcher and the wine-seller regardless of their virtue or lack thereof.
The assembly knows that the miserable realms are perilous places of sinking and drowning, where one undergoes hundreds of varieties of suffering amidst the retribution of sins;
yet when beggars come and go seeking relief and aid, it is utterly contrary to one's heart not to cease bestowing gifts.
The beggar’s request was not granted, contrary to his wishes; filled with resentment and anger, he sighed over his grievance.
This man’s heart was hard and his speech stingy; rather than relinquishing his wealth, he would even give up his life.
This person is stingy, base, and deeply deluded; they know nothing of saving others through the practice of giving.
Though they hoard wealth and goods, it will ultimately perish; yet if one practices generous charity, it shall remain forever firm and secure.
One person guards much wealth in this way; deluded and increasingly dense in ignorance, they lack reflection.
How could they know that suffering arises from false stinginess? Many people guard their possessions, yet their suffering is equal.
Neither used nor enjoyed, nor given to others—truly there is no one who recognizes this as a good thing.
Though gold and silver are piled up to fill the house, what difference is there between them and a pit filled with filth?
One who practices giving despite poverty truly fulfills the perfection of generosity; such a person is called the most eminent of men.
As for one of wealth and status who gives away a mere trifle of riches—who would not understand that this is like a single drop in a river?
If a person practices according to the Dharma without deficiency, Their fondness for giving is like their fondness for beautiful women;
If they give away their remaining wealth with continuous practice, The abundance or scarcity of the resulting fruits will likewise be so.
Purifying the field of the mind, he serves the Dharma King; In his youth, his preceptual virtue is like the fragrance of flowers.
His compassionate heart is as soft as a maiden’s; His joyful adornment makes his great conduct fragrant.
One may attend the sacred realms and practice giving, Exert diligence and cultivate much learning through bitter toil;
Yet if the rules of conduct are deficient and there is no disciplined practice, The many virtues cultivated by those who came before will all be rendered fruitless.
In this present life, one’s reputation is known and honored by others; in future lives, one is born in the heavens and revered by all.
Longevity and merit are extended afar, and one dwells in constant happiness—all these are achieved through the observance of the precepts.
I have long heard of the extreme suffering in the three miserable realms and hells; Constantly maintaining dignified deportment, my precepts and virtue are perfected.
When my life in this floating world ends and I must relinquish my breath, I shall have no fear of Yama or the evil destinies.
Whether in city-god shrines, villages, or forest retreats, whether one is deluded or wise,
and whether one knows the Dharma or not— if one seeks the Sugata, one must uphold the precepts.
Firmly maintain the prohibitive precepts to keep them pure; One must always draw near to virtuous friends.
Cultivating wholesome deeds according to the Dharma until they are perfected, All merits and virtues will gather therein.
The benefit of upholding the precepts is the attainment of peace and happiness;
if the mind is deluded and confused, one suffers injury, and one's virtue and life are extinguished in an instant. For what reason would a wise person drink alcohol?
If one drinks alcohol, manifesting folly and inferiority, ultimately committing wrongs without a good reputation,
suddenly falling to the ground as a metaphor for impermanence, with defilements overflowing the body until it becomes impure.
Though one may drink in joyful company with kinsmen, A drunken quarrel can lead to the loss of life;
Such faults arise in a single instant— Thus, this alcohol is said to be a poison more virulent than any other.
Most offenses arise from the practice of lust; even at the cost of one’s life, it still captivates the heart.
All sensual desires provide no wholesome benefit; why then do you deludedly pursue women?
If one seeks pleasure with one's own wife, it is appropriate because of constant craving and love;
yet by falsely pursuing the wives and concubines of others, one will experience loneliness and feel fear in the heart.
Flesh, blood, sinews, marrow, and the covering of skin—this body, inside and out, is entirely impure.
Even one’s own wife and children are not truly one's own; how could it be right to covet the wives of others?
If a person purifies their intent and is free from lustful desire, knowing that this union is like a phantom or a dream,
they will therefore distance themselves from women and attain peace of mind, freed from delusion.
Women can indeed provide pleasure, and the same applies to wealth, nobility, and luxury;
though one shares affection with kinsmen, life will not last long and shall soon become impermanent.
The fool increases craving one-sidedly; the wise contemplate that all is empty.
If one continues to dwell joyfully amidst the objects of attachment, when will one transcend them and attain Bodhi?
In practicing the path, do not shrink from diligent toil; it will later bring back a body of peace and happiness.
These words are truly beneficial and should be accepted and put into practice, comparable to a wondrous and excellent medicine.
All matters and actions are for the most part clear; faults and perils can all be known.
If something is fit to be done, it may be performed; how could there be any concealment regarding virtuous deeds?
If a person cultivates their future course, first eliminating the perverse and maintaining right reflection, they will certainly be free from fault at a later time;
naturally secure and at ease, suffering shall not arise.
If one cultivates wholesome karma so that it increases, with a single-minded tranquility free from frivolity,
then like an enemy or a disease of affliction, delusion will naturally be abandoned and severed.
Harsh in speech, double-tongued, and base of mind, the fool acts according to his own whims and passions;
how could he know that the majestic virtue of a peacock’s plumage is beyond comparison to the screeching of wolves, dogs, crows, and magpies?
I reprove the foolish who lack right understanding, and I extol the gates of diligence, ethical discipline, and generosity;
I say that those who practice these deeds accumulate merit and bring peace to themselves, which is supreme.
The sovereign sound of Dharma is like a song of joy; what else could one rely upon for heartless delight?
If you sentient beings turn your backs on it, will you become animals or will you remain as humans?
Neither benefit nor harm they ever perceive; Neither reality nor unreality they understand.
Thus remaining in darkness without discernment, Though possessing human form, they are no different from beasts.
Failing to distinguish between the wise and the foolish, how could one discern the jackal from the lion?
Viewing them all as equal, without regard for superiority or inferiority—the wise should not dwell with such a person for even a moment.
Not claiming to be a sage by oneself, nor being deluded; not engaging in double-tongued speech, nor being conceited;
possessing knowledge regarding the principles that are difficult to know—this is said to be the adornment of a brāhmaṇa.
With single-minded attention and subtle discernment, cultivate true practice; never at any time commit transgressions.
When arrogant and wicked people incite strife, know that such physical forms and qualities do not belong to me.
Within their deluded minds they harbor perversion; entirely lacking compassion and patience, they are full of ferocity.
Because of such arrogant faults, they cling to the notion that their own virtues surpass those of others.
Having left the household life, they hold no weight for the supreme path; they show no respect or affection whatsoever for virtuous friends;
they never offer worship to the teacher’s instructions; they care only for quarreling—truly great is their folly.
The full moon at the edge of the heavens must surely wane; The fragrant flowers beneath the mountain do not long wither.
How does the impermanence of human life differ from this? Why strive for "self" and "other"? What could one possibly achieve?
The nature of women is ultimately without reality, Obstructing people from cultivating the causes of wholesome deeds;
The āmalaka fruit possesses a seed— These are the three faults of the world.
Honoring the Dharma Master, visiting sacred sites, Practicing contentment in mind and conduct, and cherishing compassion and wisdom—
These five worldly matters, though said to be difficult to perform, are in fact easy to do.
If a person knows the Dharma and constantly practices virtue, and further seeks out virtuous friends—
just like selecting genuine gold from within the sand— they will be held in high esteem by all sentient beings.

Foolish and inferior companions lack freedom; naturally devoid of virtue and lacking respect for knowledge, should they even leave the household life, they will surely be violent and evil, and though they may survive, they will have no good reputation.
Why do you not place trust in friends?
Why do you not recognize the devas and humans?
Why do you not practice skillful means?
Why do you make it difficult for yourself to learn?
Where can a miser find the resolve for giving?
Where can there be water in shifting sands?
Where can there be fragrance in impurity?
Where can there be kindness and righteousness in an evil person?
Where can there be virtue in one who harbors both hatred and attachment?
Where can one find a virtuous person among enemies?
Who understands contentment amidst pleasure?
And who attains a long life?
The courtesan was haughty and lacked deep faith; the fool was dull-witted and devoid of discernment.
Wealth and status may flourish for a brief moment, but who can maintain them forever?
The causal nature of karma is fixed and difficult to subvert.
The Brahmin rejoices when he obtains food; the peacock rejoices at the sound of thunder;
the virtuous person rejoices in protecting others; the deluded fool rejoices when things are destroyed.
The deluded delight in engaging in strife, rejoicing like a pauper who has found treasure;
when the wise hear those skillful words, they respond like bees drawn by the fragrance of flowers.
For the virtuous person, virtue is their kin; for the transgressing person, transgression is their enemy.
For one who is treated as a lowly servant, that lowliness is suffering; for one who knows contentment, that contentment is joy.
What hesitation could there be in wandering from door to door with the alms-bowl to transform others? How could one decline the labor of serving in foreign lands?
One must never harbor the view of self regarding the body, but always harmonize the activities of the mind, making them virtuous and gentle.
With a fundamental mind free from craving and devoid of self or ego, like a deer dwelling nowhere in the wild forests;
though living amidst wealth, luxury, and high status, one should have no need to seek anything from others.
Having abandoned all pleasures derived from delusive conditions, one is entirely free from attachment and constraints,
living with a nature like that of geese and ducks, constantly moving within pure waters.
In the villages and towns where kings dwell, the eight virtues are mostly absent, with not even one or two remaining;
out of sorrowful shame for the impurity of worldly concerns, one realizes the power of the joy of non-self in all phenomena.

Amidst mountains, valleys, streams, crags, peaks, and caves, eating fruits and wearing skins while subduing the five faculties—the silent wild forests are sufficient for delight; why need one seek people in the villages?

Dwelling in the mountains, one sees no other gateways; Moving freely and joyfully without restraint, One reaps the benefit found within that mind, Subduing the sense-faculties and consciousness to attain long life.
Now that I have instructed you all, listen with palms joined and minds made supple and gentle;
the treasury of all dharmas is true peace and bliss—therein one must joyfully seek with single-minded focus.
You know that the reward for one person’s goodness is such that, if sought for even a single moment, it cannot be obtained;
yet once attained, through folly you fail to cultivate merit, remaining as before—self-destructive and sinking into the depths of saṃsāra.
A drop of water on the ground does not remain for long; it serves as a metaphor for the fragility of human life.
Who can achieve the three kinds of non-obstruction? Only those who are wise are able to practice them.
Thus, if according to his strength he applies his mind and gains even a small portion of knowledge regarding these three types [of suffering],
it is like a wild pigeon looking at its own body and thinking, "The peacock’s splendor is not superior to mine."
Who would love this impermanent cycle of birth and death? When has wisdom ever observed the five faculties?
Though this body remains, it will not last long; such a person is said to have lived in vain within the world.
Thus all see the realm of Yama; among sentient beings suffering, how many can escape?
Old age and death leave no place of peace and security uninvaded; why is it that you are unable to practice [the path]?
Impermanence should settle all sentient beings and things, yet everyone strives only for the sake of life and knows nothing else;
the path ahead has no reliance and is as fleeting as a shadow or light—why do you remain so dull-witted, failing to reflect?
Parents, wives, children, friends, and the like, Are harmonious yet illusory, existing but for a brief moment;
The true Dharma is the kinsman truly worthy of reliance, For it can lead one away from the suffering of impermanent birth and death.
Seeking much brings the reality of affliction; protecting the body brings the reality of fear;
being destroyed brings the reality of sorrow. What benefit is there for a wise person in seeking these?
If one does not cultivate the practice of True Suchness, when will the cycle of birth and death ever cease?
The wise constantly observe this world as being entirely a product of illusion and the power of delusion.
Jesting, arts, and singing are all devoid of reality; the pursuit of greed and desire is like a scabies sore.
Life is fragile and impermanent, like a phantom or a dream; how can this compare to employing one’s body and mind for the Buddha-dharma?
Yet for committing such unwholesome deeds, they all equally destroy their own bodies;
how can the minds of those in the world be so dull and dark, failing to understand that evil arises from lack of reflection?
The good and evil matters harbored within the mind are fully known by the world-protecting devas;
if one cannot contemplate this in one's heart, when will the ground of the mind ever eliminate all transgressions?
The requisites for sitting and dwelling according to conditions may provide a slight physical support for a brief time;
these auxiliary supports facilitate the practice of wholesome benefits, whereas other material possessions are merely the afflictions of people.
Though beholding magnificent palaces and the like, they have only coarse and inferior bedding;
contented and naturally joyful in heart, they regard them as if looking upon an ugly woman compared to a celestial maiden.
One must know that the conditioned wealth of this world can be seized by water, fire, and thieves;
if you seek merit for future lives, do not seek such unstable riches.
Whether in debate, commerce, agriculture, or the arts, one must not act without following the proper principles;
know that this is how it ought to be, for without merit, nothing is naturally accomplished.
Whether one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds, you should know that these are not the work of anyone else;
they are all created by the karma of one's own self, and it is through this that sentient beings obtain everything.
All such karmic actions performed, if they could prevent future existence from arising again,
then birth, old age, sickness, suffering, and impermanence would not continue to follow one after another— whence have they come?
The Sūtra of One Hundred Parables in Verse on the Conversion of the World by Vijitasena.
